lines.text: Do you know how tides work? Twice a day, whole oceans rise and fall, pulled by the Moon.
The Moon's gravity pulls on all of Earth, but hardest on the side facing it, and weakest on the far side.
That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges. One faces the Moon, and one points the opposite way.
Earth spins through both bulges every day. So most coasts get two high tides and two low tides, about every twelve hours and twenty five minutes.
The Sun pulls too, about half as strongly. At new and full moon, the Sun and Moon line up, and the tides are biggest. Those are spring tides.
When they pull at right angles, they partly cancel out, and you get smaller neap tides.
Coastlines can amplify it. In Canada's Bay of Fundy, the tide can rise more than sixteen meters.
So every high tide is the Moon, reaching down to Earth.
